results.title: We ran the same model on a B300 and a B200 last week, back to back, and watched the invoice diverge in real time. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
We ran the same model on a B300 and a B200 last week, back to back, and watched the invoice diverge in real time.

The B300 costs more per hour. $9.08 versus $7.41 for the B200, on demand. That's a 23% premium just to turn it on.

Hourly price is the wrong number to check. Cost per token is the one that matters.

We tested Llama 3.3 70B at FP4. FP4 is a compressed math format that trades a sliver of accuracy for speed. Here is what it costs on each chip:
- B300: 16,500 tokens per second, $0.055 per million tokens
- B200: 10,000 tokens per second, $0.074 per million tokens

Per token, the B300 is actually cheaper. But only past a certain volume.

The break-even sits at about 9,000 tokens per second, sustained. That works out to roughly 770 million tokens a day.

Above that line, the B300's extra speed outruns its extra price. Below it, you're paying for throughput you don't use, and the B200 wins.

Most workloads never touch 9,000 sustained tokens per second. Check yours before you upgrade.

Estimate your daily token volume and comment. We'll tell you which chip clears the break-even line.

results.title: An inference cluster running four H100s at full tilt costs $10.28 an hour. The same traffic served through a mixed setup costs $4.01 an hour, with the same tokens going out the … | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
An inference cluster running four H100s at full tilt costs $10.28 an hour. The same traffic served through a mixed setup costs $4.01 an hour, with the same tokens going out the door.

Every request has two stages. Prefill reads your prompt and builds the first output token. Decode generates every token after that, one at a time. On a 512-token response, decode eats about 80% of the wall clock.

Decode is memory-bound, not compute-bound. The GPU spends most of its time moving data rather than doing math, so a cheaper card barely loses ground there.

Split the work by stage:
- Prefill runs on the H100, where raw compute reads the prompt fast
- Decode runs on the L40S, which serves tokens for far less per hour

The full numbers: 4x H100 runs $10.28/hr at $0.89 per million tokens. A mixed cluster of 1x H100 plus 2x L40S runs $4.01/hr at $0.46 per million tokens. That is a 61% cut in hourly spend and about 48% cut in cost per token.

We wrote up the setup: vLLM 0.8+ with NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0 routing requests between the two chip types.

Read it, then tell us your current prefill/decode split.

results.title: $0.89 to fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B on an H100. $1.35 for the identical job on an MI300X. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
# $0.89 to fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B on an H100. $1.35 for the identical job on an MI300X. | Spheron Network · LinkedIn · 2026-10-02T00:00:00+00:00

**Spheron Network**.

---

$0.89 to fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B on an H100. $1.35 for the identical job on an MI300X.

The GPU with more memory and the cheaper hourly rate still lost.

MI300X looks like the obvious pick. It has 192GB of memory, more than double the H100's 80GB, and a lower price per hour. On paper, it is the easy win.

Price per hour is not the bill. The bill is price per hour multiplied by wall-clock time, the real minutes a job takes to finish, not the hours you rent the card for.

We ran the same fine-tune on both cards: Llama 3.1 8B, trained with LoRA. LoRA trains a small set of added weights instead of the whole model. That takes less memory and less time than a full fine-tune.

H100 finished in 18 minutes. MI300X took 34 minutes, almost double.

The final cost follows the clock, not the specs:

- H100: $0.89 total
- MI300X: $1.35 total, 51% more

That does not make MI300X wrong everywhere. If your model does not fit in the H100's 80GB, the extra memory still matters more than speed. For a job that fits on both cards, the bigger memory and cheaper rate still pointed the wrong way.

These figures come from our own benchmark, run in September 2026. Pricing and results may shift by region and availability. Full benchmark

results.title: There is more demand for GPUs than supply. And data centres are still underpricing their capacity. | Prashant Maurya
results.author: Prashant Maurya
highlights:
There is more demand for GPUs than supply. And data centres are still underpricing their capacity.

That sounds impossible. It isn't.

The price never reaches them intact. Capacity moves through resellers, then brokers, then brokers of brokers. Each one quotes against the next, and the only move anyone can make in the open is to go lower.

The party that owns the asset ends up knowing the least about what it's worth.
So when we built bidding into Spheron Reserve, we made one deliberate choice: you can't see anyone else's bid.

Here's how it works:
→ Every cluster lists with a base price and a ceiling
→ You place one bid anywhere in that band
→ You never see what others bid, before or after
→ An accepted bid means you get the capacity

This is a sealed-bid auction. It's not new. Spectrum licences and government contracts have run this way for decades. Krishna's Auction Theory and Milgrom's Putting Auction Theory to Work are the standard texts.

What changes is the question you're answering.

Open bidding asks: what's the lowest I can get away with?
Sealed bidding asks: what is this capacity actually worth to me?

Only the second answer tells a data centre anything useful. And with supply this tight, they're choosing who to work with as much as what to charge. A sealed bid lets them weigh both.
